transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-11-30 16:00 PT
- Duration: ~55 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Jordan Blake (MerchantEdge CTO), Samir Patel (Eng Lead), Maya Ortega (Security), Eli Torres (Platform)

Summary:
MerchantEdge is evaluating Redwood for a hybrid rollout: start with Redwood Hosted for a customer-facing recommendations endpoint, then move to Dedicated or Private for PCI-adjacent workloads. Primary concerns: latency at 2xx ms SLA for tail p95, predictable unit cost, VPC/on-prem constraints for certain merchants, and observability hooks for tracing and token-level cost attribution. They use a microservices gateway architecture today and want to understand proxy vs sidecar integration, rate limits/quotas semantics, and SDKs (official Node + Python) with LangChain / LlamaIndex connectors.

Topics covered:
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
- Gateway/proxy integration patterns and sidecar vs adapter approach
- SDK quickstarts and LangChain/LlamaIndex support
- Rate limiting, per-customer quotas, burst behavior
- Observability hooks: traces, token-level cost, rollout metrics
- Security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, SSO, audit logs

Transcript (imperfect transcription, occasional mis-heard terms):
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick agenda, we'll run through architecture, how you might integrate with Redwood, and then dig into the constraints you mentioned in your RFP.
[00:15] Jordan: Cool, thanks Alex. We're excited to see how Redwood fits. we run recommendations microservice that calls a few models, right now hosted in our own k8s cluster with some turing—sorry—turning point ops.
[00:28] Priya: Great, can you give us current traffic shape? peaks, p50/p95, average token lengths?
[00:33] Samir: Sure. typical baseline is 120 reqs/s, peaks to 900 during promos. payloads small, average prompt 80-120 tokens, sometimes long sessions for chat flows that keep context. p95 latency goal is around 200 to 250ms.
[00:47] Alex: Okay, that informs choices. Two paths: start Hosted API to get up and running fast — we have rate limit and quota primitives — or go Dedicated if you need reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput. Private (VPC/on-prem) if you need data residency or stricter network control.
[01:02] Jordan: For PCI-adjacent merchants we probably need either Dedicated with a private VPC peering or Private. How different is integration? we want to minimize code changes.
[01:12] Priya: Good question. From an integration standpoint, SDK calls are identical across modes. The main differences are networking (hosted goes over TLS to our public endpoint), and auth (hosted uses API keys and optional token scoping; Private integrates with your internal KMS and SSO). For Dedicated we still manage the control plane, but lanes are reserved so behavior is stable.
[01:33] Maya: On security, we need SOC2 docs, key rotation, and KMS/HSM support. Also audit log granularity — can you provide per-request logs with redacted payloads?
[01:43] Alex: Yes, we provide audit logs, retention options, and KMS integrations. For Private we can support customer-managed keys; for Dedicated we offer a bring-your-own-key flow with our KMS integration. We'll share SOC2 and our encryption spec after this call.
[01:56] Jordan: Good. about observability — we use datadog and open telemetry traces. How do we get token-level cost attribution back to our systems?
[02:05] Priya: We emit traces and per-request metadata. You can send a custom request_id from your gateway and we'll return it in logs and traces so you can join. Token-level cost breakdown is available in the Console and via API, and we also expose a trace link that ties tokens to latency. There's an event stream you can subscribe to for billing events.
[02:24] Eli: That sounds helpful. On the gateway pattern, we're running an API gateway (envoy) fronting microservices. Typical approach we're considering is a gateway adapter that forwards specific routes to Redwood. What's your recommended architecture?
[02:36] Priya: Two common patterns: 1) Gateway-proxy: the gateway forwards requests to Redwood's public endpoint (or through an internal proxy in Private), simple and minimal code changes; 2) Sidecar approach: inject a sidecar per service to manage batching, local cache of prompts, KV cache reuse. Sidecar is better if you want low latency and reuse of KV cache across requests inside a pod. But it adds infra overhead.
[02:54] Samir: We were hoping to offload batching to Redwood to reduce our infra. Does Redwood support continuous batching?
[03:01] Alex: Yes — our serving runtime supports continuous batching and smart routing. If you let our hosted runtime handle batching, you get better GPU utilization and lower token cost. For p95 latency-sensitive endpoints we can tune batching windows and use small-batch fast paths.
[03:16] Jordan: When you say small-batch fast path, is that model-level, sequence-length-level? how deterministic is latency under load?
[03:24] Priya: It's a combination. We pick kernels based on model, seq len, and hardware. There's a fast-path for short sequences; for long-context chats the tail will be higher. For Dedicated we give you SLA-backed latency targets and predictable capacity. We can run a benchmark during the pilot to validate p95 under your load shape.
[03:39] [break/background noise]
[03:45] Maya: If we do Private, what about network egress and merchant data leaving your infra? are we able to keep vectors in our VPC?
[03:53] Priya: For Private deployments we can keep everything inside customer networks. For Dedicated we have data isolation and can peering via VPC. We also provide a private control plane option so keys never leave your environment.
[04:05] Eli: Rate limiting — we need per-merchant quotas with bursting for promotions. How do you model quotas?
[04:12] Alex: We support hierarchical quotas: token-per-minute or reqs-per-second both at account and sub-account level. Burst token buckets are supported. You can also plug in a rate-limiter at the gateway that enforces per-merchant rules and then map to Redwood API keys with scoped quotas.
[04:26] Samir: Ok, practical SDK question: we use Node in the gateway and Python in some workers. Do you have LangChain and LlamaIndex connectors ready or do we build adapters?
[04:36] Priya: We maintain official Node and Python SDKs. There are community and Redwood-provided connectors for LangChain and Llama Index. We'll push a repo with example chains, retrievers, and the adapter for streaming responses and function/tool-calls. Expect a LangChain sample that shows a Retriever backed by Redwood embeddings and a streaming chat example.
[04:55] Jordan: Nice. Are there any gotchas with LlamaIndex and your tokenization? we've had mismatch issues in the past where token accounting off by one.
[05:04] Priya: Tokenization differences mostly come down to model choice; we surface model profiles. We'll include tokenization helpers and a token-estimation API. Also caution on KV cache semantics — if you rely on in-service KV cache naming, make sure keys are namespaced to avoid collision.
[05:21] Jordan: Heard, namespacing. About proxy vs sidecar again — if we do gateway adapter and keep state on our side, is there a recommended pattern for caching embeddings? we want to avoid recompute costs.
[05:32] Priya: Use a local embeddings cache per region + the Redwood embeddings endpoint with TTL. For shared state, you can store vector indexes in your own vector DB and use Redwood embeddings for on-demand refresh. We also support embedding cache headers so Redwood can return cache-miss hints.
[05:46] Maya: On compliance, we need encryption at rest and in transit and a clear retention policy for logs. Can you support retention rules per-tenant?
[05:53] Alex: Yes, retention is configurable; we can redact payloads automatically for certain routes and preserve metadata for audit. We'll send details.
[06:02] Samir: One more operational question — how do upgrades/rollouts work? we want canary deploys for model changes and a rollback path.
[06:09] Priya: Console supports rollouts: canary, A/B, and full rollbacks. You can pin model versions at route-level. We also support automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if latency or errors spike.
[06:21] Jordan: Excellent. On pricing, are dedicated clusters charged per GPU-hour or per-request? We want predictability for enterprise invoices.
[06:29] Alex: Dedicated is reserved capacity — committed monthly/annual with predictable baseline throughput. We invoice per-reservation SKU, with overage billed at a lower per-token rate. Hosted is usage-based per token + optional subscription components. We'll include a sample invoice scenario in the pricing doc.
[06:44] Eli: For the POC, what's the minimum we need to run a benchmark? list of endpoints, QPS profile, sample corpus?
[06:50] Priya: Yes. For the POC we need a sample traffic replay or a synthetic generator that matches your shape, list of endpoints (routes) and expected p95 SLA, plus a short list of security/network constraints. We'll provide a benchmark harness that integrates with your replay.
[07:02] Jordan: Great. Anything we should be aware of in terms of client-side SDK behavior around retries/timeouts? we had problems with double-billing on retries once.
[07:11] Priya: Good callout. Our SDKs expose idempotency keys and recommend the client set those for any non-idempotent calls. Retries are configurable and we recommend exponential backoff. We'll surface best-practices in the quickstart.
[07:26] [small crosstalk]
[07:30] Samir: For streaming, do you support chunked responses over websocket or SSE? we need to stream partial tokens to clients.
[07:38] Alex: We support streaming over SSE and websocket flavors in the SDKs. The Node SDK has a streaming client example for mobile/web flows.
[07:47] Maya: Is there an SOC2 + penetration test attestation we can include in vendor evaluation?
[07:52] Alex: Yes — we'll share SOC2 report and pen-test summary under an NDA or a secure link.
[07:59] Jordan: Okay so next steps recap? we want pricing, security docs, SDK repo, and a proposed POC plan.
[08:08] Alex: Sounds good. I'll send pricing and the dedicated vs hosted comparison. Priya will push the SDK + LangChain/LlamaIndex examples to a sample repo and message you in Slack. Maya you'll get the security packet. We'll aim to start the POC week of 2026-12-08.
[08:23] Priya: I'll also include a sample benchmark harness and a checklist of the network artifacts we need (IP allowlists, VPC peering steps if Private).
[08:31] Jordan: Perfect. any blockers from our side? Samir?
[08:34] Samir: I'll pull traffic profiles and a list of endpoints. Also will confirm whether we want sidecar experiments or gateway-first approach.
[08:41] Eli: I'll gather egress and firewall constraints, and whether we can open a peering connection to a Dedicated environment.
[08:46] Maya: I'll run the security questionnaire and flag anything that needs follow-up.
[08:50] Alex: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with docs and scheduling.

End of transcript.
